tx.t: In this talk I will explain what psychologists know about memory and how students can use it. In eighteen eighty-five, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus described the forgetting curve.

He found that people forget roughly half of new material within an hour if they do not review it. Reviewing material at increasing intervals, which is called spaced repetition, helps to move it into long-term memory.
Testing yourself is more effective than simply reading your notes again. A good night of sleep after studying helps to store what you have learned.

tx.t: Researchers at Redbridge University carried out a study in twenty twenty to find out how students prepare for exams. They followed one hundred and fifty-two students over six weeks.
On average, the students studied for seven hours a day. However, only seventy-one per cent of them used any planned method.
The students who used the method of sleeping at least eight hours made fewer mistakes in the test. The researchers concluded that how you study may matter more than how long you study.

tx.t: Today I would like to talk about the Silk Road, one of the greatest trade networks in history. It was not a single road but a network of routes connecting China with the Mediterranean.
The main routes were more than six thousand kilometres long. The Chinese envoy Zhang Qian travelled west around one hundred and thirty BC and helped to open the routes.

Cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara, in what is now Uzbekistan, became rich and famous centres of trade. Besides silk, merchants carried spices, paper, glass and precious stones, and also ideas and religions.
The routes became less important when sea trade grew cheaper in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

tx.t: In this talk I would like to tell the story of chocolate. Chocolate comes from the seeds of the cacao tree, which first grew in Central and South America.

The Maya and the Aztecs drank a bitter chocolate drink, often with chilli, and sometimes used the beans as money. Spanish explorers brought cacao to Europe in the sixteenth century, and people began to add sugar.
The first solid eating chocolate was made by an English company, Fry, in eighteen forty-seven. Milk chocolate was invented by a Swiss man, Daniel Peter, in eighteen seventy-five.

tx.t: In this lecture I will describe the Aral Sea, one of the biggest environmental disasters of the last century. The Aral Sea, between Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, was once the fourth largest lake in the world.
By two thousand and seven, the sea had lost about ninety per cent of its volume. The fishing industry collapsed, and ships were left on dry sand near the town of Moynaq.

The exposed seabed is now a desert called the Aralkum, where salty dust storms harm people's health. Today, tree planting on the old seabed and a dam in the northern part have helped to restore some of the water.

tx.t: This lecture is about the International Space Station, or ISS. The ISS orbits about four hundred kilometres above the Earth.
It travels at roughly twenty-eight thousand kilometres an hour, so it circles the Earth about every ninety minutes. That means the crew sees about sixteen sunrises every day.
People have lived on board continuously since November two thousand. Without gravity, muscles and bones become weaker, so astronauts exercise for about two hours a day.

In eighteen forty-eight, the population was about five thousand. Over the next fifty years it grew to twenty-one thousand.
Then things changed, because the main road was moved outside the centre. As a result, fewer travellers passed through the market.
